micros.title: Warm-up: Four Operations on Rationals
micros.description: Revise adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers in fraction form, including negatives.
outcomes: Can compute a±b, a×b, a÷b for any two rationals
Can handle signs correctly through each operation

micros.title: Closure, Commutativity and Associativity
micros.description: Test which of the four operations keep rationals closed, commutative and associative — and catch subtraction and division failing the last two.
outcomes: Can state which properties hold for which operations
Can produce a counterexample when a property fails

question.prompt: Which of these is TRUE for rational numbers?

options.text: a − b = b − a for all rationals a, b
a ÷ b = b ÷ a whenever both sides are defined
a × b = b × a for all rationals a, b
(a − b) − c = a − (b − c) for all rationals
options.diagnosis: Assumed associativity extends to subtraction; try a=5, b=3, c=1: 1 ≠ 3.

question.explanation: Only addition and multiplication are commutative and associative for rationals. Check 3 − 5 = −2 but 5 − 3 = 2, and 1 ÷ 2 ≠ 2 ÷ 1. One counterexample kills a property.

micros.title: Identities, Opposites and Reciprocals
micros.description: Fix 0 and 1 as the additive and multiplicative identities, and sharply separate the additive inverse (opposite) from the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) — noting 0 has no reciprocal.
outcomes: Can give the additive and multiplicative inverse of any rational
Can explain why 0 has no reciprocal

question.prompt: What is the multiplicative inverse (reciprocal) of −5/8?

options.diagnosis: Flipped the fraction but also flipped the sign — a reciprocal keeps the sign, since the product must be +1.

question.explanation: The reciprocal r must satisfy (−5/8) × r = 1, so r = −8/5. The OPPOSITE of −5/8 is 5/8 (sums to 0) — that is the additive inverse, a different job. And 0 never works: nothing times 0 gives 1.

micros.title: Distributivity and Smart Computation
micros.description: Use a(b + c) = ab + ac to reorganise messy rational calculations into easy ones.
outcomes: Can apply distributivity to simplify computations like 3/7 × 5/6 + 3/7 × 1/6

micros.title: Rationals on the Number Line
micros.description: Locate any rational, positive or negative, on the number line by subdividing unit intervals.
outcomes: Can mark rationals like −7/4 on a number line accurately

micros.title: Density: Rationals Between Rationals
micros.description: Discover that between ANY two rationals lie infinitely many more, using averages and common denominators.
outcomes: Can find n rationals between two given rationals
Can argue why the process never runs out

question.prompt: How many rational numbers lie between 1/4 and 1/2?

options.text: Only those with denominator 4: none in this case
options.diagnosis: Restricted attention to one denominator; rewriting as 2/8 and 4/8, then 4/16 and 8/16, keeps exposing new rationals.

question.explanation: The average of two distinct rationals is a new rational strictly between them, and you can average again forever: 1/4 < 3/8 < 1/2, then 1/4 < 5/16 < 3/8, ... Rationals are dense.

micros.title: Perfect Squares and Their Fingerprints
micros.description: Generate squares 1–30 and read off their properties: possible unit digits, behaviour of trailing zeros, and sums of odd numbers.
outcomes: Can list unit digits a perfect square can end in
Can reject candidates like 4058 as perfect squares by inspection

question.prompt: Exactly one of these numbers is a perfect square. Which one COULD it be, judging by unit digits?

options.diagnosis: Ends in 7 — no square ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, so it is ruled out immediately.

question.explanation: A perfect square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. Endings 3, 8 and 7 disqualify the other three instantly; 5776 ends in 6 and is in fact 76². The unit-digit test rejects, it never confirms — but here it leaves only one candidate.

micros.title: Squaring Fractions and Decimals
micros.description: Square rationals like 3/4 and 0.4, tracking why squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it SMALLER and where the decimal point lands.
outcomes: Can square any fraction or decimal correctly
Can explain why (0.4)² < 0.4

question.prompt: Compute: (0.4)²

options.diagnosis: Squared 4 but dropped the decimal point entirely.

question.explanation: (0.4)² = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16 — two decimal places in, two + two = ... count decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2 places, giving 0.16. Squaring is NOT doubling (that would be 0.8), and 4² = 16 must keep its decimal shift.

micros.title: Square Roots by Prime Factorisation
micros.description: Find square roots of perfect squares by pairing prime factors, and find the smallest multiplier/divisor that makes a number a perfect square.
outcomes: Can compute √ of a perfect square via factor pairs
Can find the least number to multiply by to reach a perfect square

micros.title: Square Roots by Long Division
micros.description: Use the long-division algorithm for square roots of large perfect squares and decimals.
outcomes: Can extract √ of 4-5 digit numbers by long division
Can extend the method past the decimal point

micros.title: Estimating Square Roots
micros.description: Trap non-perfect squares between consecutive perfect squares to estimate roots like √60 ≈ 7.7.
outcomes: Can state between which two integers √n lies
Can give a one-decimal estimate of a square root

micros.title: √ Does Not Split Over + and −
micros.description: Confront the error √(a+b) = √a + √b with numeric ambushes like √(9+16), and establish that roots split only over × and ÷.
outcomes: Can evaluate √(a+b) correctly by adding first
Can state for which operations √ distributes

question.prompt: Evaluate: √(9 + 16)

options.diagnosis: Halved 25 — treated square-rooting as halving.
Added correctly but forgot to take the root at all.

question.explanation: Add first: 9 + 16 = 25, and √25 = 5. Splitting gives √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7 — a different, wrong number. The root distributes over × (√(9×16) = 3×4 = 12 ✓) but never over + or −.

micros.title: Cubes and Their Patterns
micros.description: Build cubes 1–20 as n × n × n (not n × 3), and explore unit-digit patterns — cubes, unlike squares, can end in ANY digit.
outcomes: Can compute cubes of numbers up to 20
Can state the unit digit of a cube from the unit digit of the number

question.prompt: Compute: 4³

options.diagnosis: Squared instead of cubed — stopped one multiplication early.
Computed 3⁴ (or a wrong table fact) — swapped base and exponent.

question.explanation: 4³ means 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. The exponent counts how many copies of 4 are multiplied — it is never a multiplier itself (that would be 4 × 3 = 12).

micros.title: Cubes of Negative Numbers
micros.description: Establish that an odd number of negative factors leaves the product negative: cubing preserves sign.
outcomes: Can cube negative integers and rationals correctly
Can explain the sign via counting negative factors

question.prompt: Compute: (−5)³

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by 3 AND applied the even-power sign rule — two errors stacked.

question.explanation: (−5)³ = (−5)(−5)(−5): the first pair gives +25, the third factor flips it to −125. THREE negative signs — an odd count — always leave a negative product. Even powers kill the sign; odd powers keep it.

micros.title: Cube Roots by Prime Factorisation
micros.description: Find cube roots by grouping prime factors in TRIPLES, and find the smallest multiplier that turns a number into a perfect cube.
outcomes: Can compute ∛ of a perfect cube via factor triples
Can find the least factor needed to complete a perfect cube

question.prompt: Find: ∛216

options.diagnosis: Took the square root instead of the cube root.

question.explanation: 216 = 2×2×2 × 3×3×3 = (2×3)³, so ∛216 = 6. Check: 6×6×6 = 216. Dividing by 3 (216 ÷ 3 = 72) or halving are answers to different questions — a root undoes REPEATED MULTIPLICATION, not multiplication by 3.

micros.title: Estimating Cube Roots of Perfect Cubes
micros.description: Use the unit digit and thousands-grouping trick to read off cube roots of perfect cubes up to six digits.
outcomes: Can find ∛ of a 4-6 digit perfect cube by the two-group estimation method

micros.title: Warm-up: Ratios and Percentage Change
micros.description: Revise converting between fractions, ratios and per cents, and computing increase/decrease as a percentage of the ORIGINAL value.
outcomes: Can find x% of a quantity and a percentage change
Can identify the base quantity a per cent acts on

micros.title: Discount and Marked Price
micros.description: Work the trio marked price, discount, sale price — the discount per cent always bites the MARKED price.
outcomes: Can compute sale price from MP and discount %
Can recover MP or discount % from the other two

question.prompt: A jacket is marked ₹800 and sold at a 15% discount. What is the sale price?

options.diagnosis: Subtracted ₹15 — treated the per cent as a rupee amount.
Computed the discount amount but reported it as the sale price — stopped a step early.

question.explanation: Discount = 15% of the MARKED price = 0.15 × 800 = ₹120, so sale price = 800 − 120 = ₹680. (₹692 comes from discounting some other base, e.g. taking 15% off ₹800 minus tax or applying 13.5%: the discount must act on ₹800 itself.)

micros.title: Successive Percentage Changes
micros.description: Chain two percentage changes multiplicatively and see why 10% off then 20% off is 28% off — never 30% — and why +10% then −10% does not restore the price.
outcomes: Can compute the net effect of two successive % changes
Can explain why successive per cents don't add

question.prompt: A shop gives successive discounts of 10% and then 20% on a ₹1000 item. What is the final price?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the discount fractions instead of the REMAINING fractions (0.90 and 0.80).
Applied 10% then 20% but computed the second discount on ₹1000 again instead of on ₹900.

question.explanation: After 10% off: 1000 × 0.90 = ₹900. After 20% off THAT: 900 × 0.80 = ₹720. Net effect 28% off, not 30% — the second discount acts on an already-reduced price, so successive per cents multiply (0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72), never add.

micros.title: Sales Tax, VAT and GST
micros.description: Add tax percentages onto bills and extract the pre-tax price from a tax-inclusive total.
outcomes: Can compute a bill including tax
Can find the original price given a tax-inclusive amount

micros.title: Compound Interest: Interest on Interest
micros.description: Contrast CI with SI year by year on the same principal, then compress the growth into A = P(1 + r/100)ⁿ.
outcomes: Can compute CI for 2-3 years both stepwise and by formula
Can say exactly where CI and SI diverge and why

question.prompt: ₹1000 is invested at 10% per annum, compounded annually. How much interest has it earned after 2 years?

options.diagnosis: Computed only one year's interest.
Reported the final AMOUNT instead of the interest earned.

question.explanation: Year 1: 10% of 1000 = ₹100, balance ₹1100. Year 2: 10% of 1100 = ₹110 — interest now earns interest. Total ₹210. Simple interest would pay 10% of the ORIGINAL ₹1000 both years: ₹200. The ₹10 gap is exactly the interest on year 1's interest.

micros.title: CI Applications: Growth and Depreciation
micros.description: Apply the compound formula to population growth, bacterial growth and depreciation (negative rate), including half-yearly compounding.
outcomes: Can adapt A = P(1 ± r/100)ⁿ to growth and depreciation contexts
Can halve the rate and double the periods for half-yearly compounding

micros.title: Warm-up: Laws of Exponents
micros.description: Revise aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ with positive exponents — exponents ADD and SUBTRACT, they are never multiplied or divided across the laws.
outcomes: Can apply the product and quotient laws with positive integer exponents

question.prompt: Simplify: a⁸ ÷ a²

options.diagnosis: Added the exponents — used the product law on a quotient.
Divided the bases as well as handling the exponents — the base a stays.

question.explanation: a⁸ ÷ a² cancels two of the eight factors of a, leaving a⁶: exponents SUBTRACT (8 − 2 = 6). Dividing them (8 ÷ 2 = 4) answers a different question — write out the factors once and the cancellation is visible.

micros.title: What a Negative Exponent Means
micros.description: Extend the descending pattern 2³, 2², 2¹, 2⁰, ... to force 2⁻ⁿ = 1/2ⁿ: a negative exponent flips into a reciprocal, it never makes the value negative.
outcomes: Can evaluate powers with negative exponents
Can explain 2⁻³ = 1/8 via the halving pattern

question.prompt: Evaluate: 2⁻³

options.diagnosis: Flipped to the reciprocal AND attached a minus sign — the flip alone does the whole job.

question.explanation: Follow the pattern: 2³=8, 2²=4, 2¹=2, 2⁰=1, and each step divides by 2 — so 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4, 2⁻³ = 1/8. The minus sign in the exponent means 'reciprocal', not 'negative': 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8, a positive number.

micros.title: Exponent Laws with Negative Exponents
micros.description: Run all the laws — product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product — with integer (including negative) exponents.
outcomes: Can simplify expressions like (2⁻³ × 2⁷) ÷ 2² fully
Can combine laws in multi-step simplifications

micros.title: Standard Form for Large Numbers
micros.description: Write large numbers like 149,600,000 km as a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10, counting decimal SHIFTS rather than zeros.
outcomes: Can convert large numbers to standard form and back
Can compare two numbers written in standard form

micros.title: Standard Form for Small Numbers
micros.description: Use negative powers of 10 for very small measurements (0.00052 m = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ m), pinning down the sign and size of the exponent by counting shifts.
outcomes: Can convert small decimals to standard form with the right negative exponent

question.prompt: Write 0.00052 in standard form.

options.diagnosis: The power is consistent, but standard form needs the leading factor between 1 and 10 — 52 is too big.

question.explanation: Move the decimal point until one nonzero digit leads: 0.00052 → 5.2 needs 4 shifts right, so the exponent is −4 (small number ⇒ negative power). Counting the three zeros gives −3, one off: count SHIFTS of the point, not zeros. Check: 5.2 × 10⁻⁴ = 5.2 ÷ 10000 = 0.00052.

micros.title: Direct or Inverse? Recognising the Relationship
micros.description: Sort real situations by asking 'when one doubles, does the other double or halve?' — and spot relationships that are NEITHER.
outcomes: Can classify a situation as direct, inverse, or neither
Can justify the classification with a doubling test

question.prompt: Which situation shows INVERSE proportion?

options.text: More pipes filling a tank, less time to fill it
More metres of cloth, higher total cost
options.diagnosis: That is DIRECT proportion — both grow together.

options.text: A child's age and their height
More workers on a job, more days to finish

question.explanation: Inverse proportion: doubling one quantity HALVES the other, keeping the product constant — twice the pipes, half the time. Cloth/cost is direct (constant ratio). Age/height grows together but with no fixed ratio — proportional thinking doesn't apply at all there.

micros.title: Solving Direct Proportion Problems
micros.description: Set up x/y = constant (or the unitary method) for direct variation — a multiplicative relationship, not 'add the same amount'.
outcomes: Can solve for the missing value in a direct proportion
Can verify the answer keeps the ratio constant

question.prompt: A car uses 6 litres of petrol for 90 km. How far can it travel on 10 litres?

options.diagnosis: Multiplied 90 by 6/10 instead of 10/6 — inverted the scale factor.
Multiplied 90 × 10 without dividing by 6 — skipped the unitary step.

question.explanation: Distance per litre is constant: 90 ÷ 6 = 15 km/L, so 10 L gives 150 km. The relationship is multiplicative (×10/6), not additive — '4 more litres so 4 more km' (94) treats it as y = x + k.

micros.title: Solving Inverse Proportion Problems
micros.description: Use x₁y₁ = x₂y₂ — the PRODUCT stays constant — for inverse variation, resisting both the additive shortcut and the direct-proportion reflex.
outcomes: Can solve for the missing value in an inverse proportion
Can check the answer by comparing products

question.prompt: 6 workers can build a wall in 12 days. Working at the same rate, how long would 8 workers take?

options.diagnosis: Adjusted additively in the wrong direction — added the 2 extra workers to the days.

question.explanation: Total work = 6 × 12 = 72 worker-days; with 8 workers, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 days. The PRODUCT stays fixed, so more workers ⇒ proportionally fewer days. Scaling up (16) applies direct proportion; '2 more workers, 2 fewer days' (10) pretends the trade-off is additive.

micros.title: Mixed and Multi-step Proportion Problems
micros.description: Tackle problems mixing both variation types (speed-time-distance, recipes scaled for more people in less time), choosing the model before computing.
outcomes: Can solve two-step problems involving both direct and inverse variation

micros.title: Numbers in General Form
micros.description: Write any two- or three-digit numeral algebraically — 'ab' means 10a + b, never a × b — and use it to explain simple number tricks.
outcomes: Can expand a numeral into general form and back
Can express 'reverse the digits' algebraically

question.prompt: A two-digit number has tens digit a and units digit b. Which expression equals the number?

options.diagnosis: Summed the digits — that loses the place value entirely (72 would equal 9).
Right structure, wrong places — this is the REVERSED number.

question.explanation: The tens digit counts tens: 7 tens and 2 units is 10×7 + 2 = 72. Writing digits side by side is positional notation, not multiplication — a×b for 72 would give 14.

micros.title: Adding and Subtracting Reversed Numbers
micros.description: Prove with general form why (10a+b) + (10b+a) is always divisible by 11, and the difference by 9 — the classic reversal results.
outcomes: Can prove the 11 and 9 divisibility facts for reversed two-digit numbers
Can extend the argument to three-digit reversals (divisibility by 99)

micros.title: Letters for Digits: Cryptarithm Puzzles
micros.description: Solve addition and multiplication puzzles where letters stand for digits, respecting the rules: one digit per letter, 0-9 only, carries tracked, no leading zeros.
outcomes: Can solve one- and two-carry cryptarithms systematically
Can state and use the digit constraints explicitly

question.prompt: In the puzzle A1 + 1B = B0 (each letter one digit, B0 a two-digit number), what is A?

options.diagnosis: Ignored the carry from the units column: 1 + B ends in 0 forces B = 9 WITH a carry into the tens.
Made the sum's tens work without carrying, but then A1 has a leading-zero problem and the units column fails.

question.explanation: Units: 1 + B ends in 0, so B = 9, carry 1. Tens: A + 1 + 1(carry) = B = 9, so A = 7. Check: 71 + 19 = 90. ✓ Every letter must stay a single digit 0-9 and every carry must be honoured.

micros.title: Why the Divisibility Tests Work
micros.description: Use general form to justify the tests for 2, 5, 10 (last digit) and 3, 9 (digit sum) — and see why 3's test looks at ALL digits, and why divisible-by-3 does not mean divisible-by-9.
outcomes: Can apply the tests for 2, 3, 5, 9, 10 correctly
Can explain via 10 = 9 + 1 why digit sums govern 3 and 9

question.prompt: Which of these numbers is divisible by 9?

options.diagnosis: Ends in 8, an even digit — but evenness tests 2, not 9; digit sum 28 is not a multiple of 9.

question.explanation: Test with digit sums: 3+4+3+8 = 18, a multiple of 9, so 3438 works (3438 = 9 × 382). 1279 contains a 9 but its digit sum is 19 — a 9 'anywhere' proves nothing. 1236 has digit sum 12: divisible by 3, NOT by 9 — the 3-test passing never guarantees the 9-test.

micros.title: Warm-up: Transposing with Inverse Operations
micros.description: Revise solving ax + b = c by moving terms with their operations INVERTED — plus becomes minus, times becomes divide.
outcomes: Can solve one-side linear equations fluently
Can name the inverse operation used at each step

micros.title: Variables on Both Sides
micros.description: Collect variable terms on one side and constants on the other, changing the SIGN of every term that crosses the equals sign.
outcomes: Can solve equations like 2x + 5 = x + 9
Can verify a solution by substitution

question.prompt: Solve: 2x + 5 = x + 9

options.diagnosis: Reached 2x = 4 by also moving the x with its sign unchanged, then divided — check by substituting: 9 ≠ 11.

question.explanation: Move x left and 5 right, flipping signs: 2x − x = 9 − 5, so x = 4. Check: 2(4)+5 = 13 = 4+9. ✓ Every term that crosses '=' swaps sign; x = 14 keeps +5 alive as +5, and x = 4/3 comes from 2x + x = 4.

micros.title: Equations with Brackets
micros.description: Expand brackets — multiplying EVERY term inside — before collecting, as in 3(x − 2) = 2(x + 1) + 1.
outcomes: Can solve equations with bracketed terms on either side

micros.title: Clearing Fractions
micros.description: Multiply BOTH SIDES — every single term — by the LCM of the denominators to turn fractional equations into integer ones.
outcomes: Can clear denominators correctly and solve
Can spot the error of multiplying only the fraction term

question.prompt: Solve: x/2 + 3 = 5

options.diagnosis: Computed (5 − 3) ÷ 2 — divided by 2 at the end instead of multiplying.
Multiplied through by 2 twice — once clearing, once again at the end.

question.explanation: Multiply EVERY term by 2: x + 6 = 10, so x = 4. Check: 4/2 + 3 = 5. ✓ Multiplying only the x/2 term gives x + 3 = 10 ⇒ x = 7 — but then the two sides were scaled unequally, breaking the equation.

micros.title: Equations Reducible to Linear Form
micros.description: Solve equations like (x + 1)/(2x + 3) = 3/8 by cross-multiplication, checking the solution keeps denominators nonzero.
outcomes: Can cross-multiply and solve rational equations that reduce to linear
Can reject values that zero a denominator

micros.title: Word Problems: Set Up, Solve, ANSWER
micros.description: Translate age, number, perimeter and money stories into equations — then finish: solve fully and answer the question actually asked.
outcomes: Can model a word problem as a linear equation
Can present the final answer in the problem's terms, checked against the story

question.prompt: Sum of two numbers is 95. One exceeds the other by 15. The problem asks for the SMALLER number. You reach x + (x + 15) = 95. What is the answer?

options.diagnosis: Restated a given from the problem instead of solving.

question.explanation: 2x + 15 = 95 ⇒ 2x = 80 ⇒ x = 40, and x was DEFINED as the smaller number. 55 is the larger one — a correct solve answering the wrong question. And '2x = 80' is a checkpoint, not an answer: always finish, then reread what was asked.
